Some reviewers appreciated the model formulation and empirical tests, and think that the model represents a step forward for oscillatory networks. The main concern was that the authors do not properly situate their work within the context of the somewhat extensive existing literature on oscillatory models. The authors promised to revise their paper to properly situate their work, which satisfied the reviewers. Provided the authors revise their work as promised, I recommend acceptance.

author_final_remarks.value:
In this work, we propose BioOSS, a wave-based, PDE-grounded, bio-inspired local coupling mechanism with spatiotemporal dependencies. By discretizing and diagonalizing the spatial operator via eigendecomposition and approximating its eigenvectors, we adapt a wave PDE—commonly used for spatial wave-propagation simulation—to be directly parameterized by trainable variables (wave speed and damping coefficient) and made compatible with the SSM architecture, thereby avoiding per-step spatial operator computation. This design substantially improves computational efficiency while preserving the inductive bias of local wave coupling, achieving competitive performance across diverse time-series tasks. Moreover, this formulation enables calculation of the eigenfrequency at each grid in the 2D neural network, enhancing the biological interpretability of the learned spatiotemporal dynamics.

We sincerely thank the reviewers for their constructive and insightful feedback, which has greatly enhanced both the clarity and technical depth of our work. Their comments enabled us to improve the experimental design, refine the presentation of our core contributions, and strengthen the related work discussion. We have addressed all major concerns during the rebuttal and discussion phases and will incorporate the suggested clarifications, additional citations, ablation studies, and presentation enhancements into the final version. We believe these revisions will further strengthen the manuscript.

The point about the UEA and PPG dataset splits varying between python environments is somewhat concerning. Specifically, it is the random seed that determines the splits for the Rusch and Walker papers, and this split is very important in our experience. Because these datasets are so small, the test performance of the model varies drastically based on the split chosen, and therefore 'tuning the random seed' for the dataset split can very easily make one model look better than another. It is unfortunate that the field has settled on a very specific random split of this dataset for evaluation, without actually publishing this dataset, but that is the way it is. We encourage the authors to run the experiments with exactly the same Jax version as the Rusch et al. library (or Walker's code) to ensure that the split is the same for the camera ready.

We thank the reviewer for their continued engagement and for raising insightful follow-up questions. Below, we address each point in turn.

**Comment 1:** *“It would be important to make the promised edits in the paper.”*

**Response:**  
We will include all promised edits in the final version. In particular:

- Clarify that BioOSS's core contribution lies in introducing a **new mechanism for generating oscillations**, grounded in a first-order PDE formulation, rather than proposing SOTA SSM;
- Emphasize the differences from LinOSS in theoretical formulation (PDE vs second-order ODE), spatial structure (2D grid vs 1D vector), and recurrence behavior;
- Improve citation clarity and cross-referencing, especially where structural similarities (e.g., scan, algorithm blocks) may lead to confusion.

**Comment 2:** *“I don't understand this statement: 'While approximate, the parameters c and k are trainable, allowing backpropagation to correct for errors.' How would backprop correct any deviations from the original PDE, since we do not train to approximate the PDE?”*

**Response:**  
To enable efficient scan-based recurrence, the update matrix $A = M_{\text{Damp}}^{-1} M_{\text{Velocity}}$ must be diagonalized as $A = P \Lambda P^{-1}$.  
However, computing $P$ exactly would require re-evaluating divergence and gradient operators at every step, which is computationally expensive and non-differentiable.

We resolve this by using a **physically grounded approximation**: both $P$ and $\Lambda$ are expressed analytically as functions of the trainable parameters $c$ and $k$. This approximation retains the structure and interpretability of wave dynamics while enabling fast, parallelizable updates via the scan operation.

Since $c$ and $k$ are updated during training, both $P$ and $\Lambda$ evolve implicitly. Backpropagation adjusts wave speed and damping to match the task objective. We will clarify this mechanism in Section 3.3 of the final version.

**Comment 3:** *“Performances in Table 1: Did you use the same training and fine-tuning protocol for all models, i.e., S5, LRU, and LinOSS, and BioOSS? Can you please provide details on that?”*

**Response:**  
We used the official LinOSS codebase but encountered dependency issues in the original environment. After reconstructing the setup, we were able to train the model; however, the reproduced results differed significantly from those reported in the original paper. To address this, we rebuilt the environment to approximate the original performance as closely as possible, though some float remains. Notably, our reproduction on the SCP2 dataset even exceeds the originally reported result. Our intention is not to downplay LinOSS’s performance.

We did not perform a dedicated grid search for LinOSS, whereas BioOSS includes learning rate tuning due to its internal complexity. This may also contribute to observed performance differences.

We do not question the validity of the original LinOSS results. In the final version, we will clarify:
- That LinOSS and other baselines were evaluated using their official implementations;
- That performance deviations may arise from environment differences and a lack of hyperparameter tuning;
- That our aim was not to re-evaluate LinOSS, but to benchmark all models under a unified protocol.

Finally, our paper does not present BioOSS as a new SOTA. We consistently describe its performance as **competitive**, not superior. Our goal is to explore whether biologically interpretable oscillatory dynamics can be effectively integrated into general-purpose modeling frameworks.

We address the reviewer’s remaining concerns below:

**1. On the claim that BioOSS is the only 'PDE-derived' model:**

We acknowledge the reviewer’s (and rG4F’s) concern and clarify that our intent was not to claim BioOSS is the *only* PDE-based model. Rather, we aim to highlight the distinct way in which BioOSS employs PDEs to model local coupling, particularly in contrast to NWM. To avoid potential misunderstandings, we have revised the manuscript as follows:

> Recent models have explored oscillatory and wave-like computation in neural systems using varied abstractions. Neural Wave Machines (NWM), for example, simulate traveling waves by arranging neurons on a topographic grid and applying circular convolutional kernels (initialized as shift operators) to implement one-dimensional propagation. These learned couplings, combined with oscillatory recurrence from a coRNN base, yield traveling wave dynamics (Keller & Welling, 2023).
>
> BioOSS, by contrast, formulates coupled partial differential equations (PDEs) over a two-dimensional neural grid, modeling interactions between signal-bearing units and modulatory units. This setup is loosely inspired by structural and functional motifs in prefrontal microcircuits, where local propagation is shaped by spatial diffusion and laminar organization (Watakabe et al., 2023).
>
> Both models abstract biological dynamics differently. BioOSS emphasizes spatially structured, trainable propagation and damping, supporting locally modulated oscillations. While NWM uses learned convolutional recurrence in discrete time, BioOSS derives recurrence from a discretized PDE system, enabling closed-form eigendecomposition and Fourier-domain analysis to justify scan-efficient updates and characterize frequency-specific responses.
>
> The PDE formulation yields a diverse spectrum of localized oscillatory modes, modulated by trainable spatial parameters like damping and wave speed. This diversity enables richer internal dynamics than architectures relying solely on learned recurrence. Consequently, BioOSS is well suited for tasks with inherent temporal periodicity or resonance.

**2. On the visualization of wave dynamics:**

In the final version, we will include short GIF animations for several test samples, generated using trained checkpoints. These visualizations will demonstrate the spatiotemporal evolution of the model's internal states and illustrate the wave-like behavior more effectively.

**3. On the connection to Watakabe et al.:**

We agree with the reviewer that the connection to Watakabe et al. (2023) is primarily motivational. Our intention was not to claim that BioOSS fully implements the mechanisms described in their work, but rather to point out that, compared to prior models, the architectural motifs in BioOSS—such as the separation between signal and modulatory units and the spatial coupling—are more closely aligned with the structural and functional patterns reported by Watakabe et al. And the cited work proposes plausible laminar organization and connectivity patterns but does not preclude alternative mechanisms. Our model was inspired by the suggested architectural motifs but does not claim to fully implement the connectivity described in their work.

**4. On dataset splits and reproducibility (Question 5):**

For the UEA and PPG datasets, we used the LinOSS codebase by Rusch et al. All dataset splits and random seeds are identical to those in their official implementation. However, results can vary across Python environments. We selected a Python environment that yielded the best overall performance. While some results may differ slightly from the original reports, all splits and seeds were kept identical to ensure a fair comparison.

For the datasets used in Table 3, we followed the dataset preparation and evaluation protocol from the publicly released codebase of "CycleNet: Enhancing Time Series Forecasting through Modeling Periodic Patterns." Again, all dataset splits and seeds are exactly as provided in the original benchmark. These clarifications will be included in the appendix.

We thank the authors for their careful response to our review. We include a few comments below.

- The ablation study is most welcomed and very appreciated. 
- We also appreciate the clarifications the reviewer has made in regards to related work and biological plausibility. The separation of signal and modulation is indeed quite novel with respect to prior work, and so we appreciate the authors highlighting this.

We have some remaining concerns:

First, we do not believe it is quite appropriate to say BioOSS is the only ‘PDE derived’ model. Even the coupling in the NWM can be seen to be derived from a finite difference approximation to a local gradient operator, turning the system into a PDE approximation as well. 

Second, long sequence lengths do not preclude the use of gifs or videos in the supplementary material to demonstrate wave dynamics. Just because the system can support traveling waves does not mean that they will necessarily emerge in training. Thus if the authors wish to refer to them extensively in the text, they should be demonstrated visually or quantitatively. 

Third, the connection to Watakabe et al still seemed stretched. If anything it seems it is motivational rather than mechanistic in its relation to the proposed BioOSS model. 

Finally, with respect to question 5, can the authors clarify more precisely how they do the split? Do they use the code base of Walker or Rusch? Do they use the exact same random seeds? This is quite important to the interpretation of the results.

> BioOSS, by contrast, formulates **coupled partial differential equations (PDEs)** over a two-dimensional neural grid, modeling interactions between signal-bearing units ($p$) and modulatory units ($o$). This setup is loosely inspired by structural and functional motifs in prefrontal microcircuits (Watakabe et al., 2023), where local propagation is shaped by spatial diffusion and laminar organization.  
>  
> Both models abstract biological dynamics differently. BioOSS emphasizes spatially structured, trainable propagation and damping, supporting locally modulated oscillations. While NWM uses learned convolutional recurrence in discrete time, BioOSS derives recurrence from a discretized PDE system, enabling **closed-form eigendecomposition** and Fourier-domain analysis to justify scan-efficient updates and characterize frequency-specific responses.  
>  
> The PDE formulation yields a **diverse spectrum of localized oscillatory modes**, modulated by trainable spatial parameters like damping ($k$) and wave speed ($c$). This diversity enables **richer internal dynamics** than architectures relying solely on learned recurrence. Consequently, BioOSS is well suited for tasks with **inherent temporal periodicity or resonance**.

We will revise the manuscript to clarify these distinctions and avoid unintended implications of superiority over related models such as NWM.

## 2. Clarification on the Role of the Fourier Domain in Training

Section 3.3 presents an efficient solution of the PDE system in the Fourier domain via eigendecomposition of matrix $A$, but we clarify that this formulation is **integral to training**, not merely analytical.

### Motivation: Scan efficiency through diagonalization

The system matrix $A = M_{\text{Damp}}^{-1} M_{\text{Velocity}}$ is generally **non-diagonal** in the spatial domain, making scan operations in Eq. 18 inefficient. To address this, we compute the **eigendecomposition** $A = P \Lambda P^{-1}$, where $\Lambda$ is diagonal with complex eigenvalues governing local oscillations. This allows scan operations to be applied efficiently to $\Lambda$, with $P$ and $P^{-1}$ used to transform the hidden state between spatial and frequency domains.

### Practical implementation

This diagonalized formulation is **used during training**. We cache $P$, $P^{-1}$, and $\Lambda$ and use them to update recurrence in the temporal loop. This eliminates repeated full matrix operations, making the model **scan compatible** and reducing computation per timestep.

### Oscillatory interpretation as a secondary benefit

In addition to its computational role, the Fourier-domain view also allows us to **characterize internal dynamics** by interpreting each neuron's eigenvalue as a localized oscillator with a specific frequency. This underpins our analysis of frequency selectivity (Fig. 2, Eq. 21), but is **secondary to the primary goal** of improving the model's interpretability.

We will revise Section 3.3 to clarify the dual role of the Fourier-domain formulation in both training and interpretability.

## 3. Clarification on $\pi$ vs $2\pi$ in Frequency Interpretation

We thank the reviewer for noting this. While $2\pi$ is standard for continuous-time angular frequency, our model operates in **discrete time** with real-valued recurrence governed by complex eigenvalue pairs: $\lambda = re^{\pm i\theta}$.

The resulting signal follows:

$$
x[n] = A \cos(\theta n) + B \sin(\theta n)
$$

Though the full period is $2\pi / \theta$, we observe that **waveform symmetry** makes $\pi$ a more intuitive reference for **oscillatory behavior**, since the envelope and pattern repeat every $\pi$ radians. Hence, we use:

$$
f = \frac{\theta}{\pi \Delta t}
$$

as a **frequency proxy**. This aids interpretation of resonance and aligns with empirical selectivity plots (e.g., Fig. 2).

We will clarify this choice in Section 3.5 to prevent confusion with conventional frequency definitions.

We thank the reviewer for their constructive feedback. We address the main concerns and clarify key distinctions with prior literature.

## Major Concern 1: Missing Related Work and Comparison to Similar Models

We acknowledge the need for a more comprehensive discussion of prior works. Due to space limits, our original submission focused on comparing to LinOSS, the most structurally similar SSM model. In the final version, we will expand the Related Work section to clarify how BioOSS differs in **mechanism**, **biology**, and **tasks**. As reviewer rG4F raised the same issue, we will expand the Related Work section using the revisions outlined in our response to rG4F.

## Major Concern 2: Lack of Ablation Studies and Justification for Architectural Components

**Reviewer:** It is unclear what the contribution of the $o$ neurons is, and how the proposed model differs from LinOSS + local coupling or NWM. No ablations are shown.

**Response:** 

### Clarifying the Contribution of $o$ Neurons

$O$ neurons in **BioOSS** modulate the spatiotemporal dynamics of $p$ neurons, which propagate signals. This two-field setup is inspired by the FDTD method, where interleaved state variables (e.g., pressure and velocity) enable wave propagation. Analogously, BioOSS separates signal transmission ($p$ neurons) from modulation ($o$ neurons), enabling control over wave speed and damping across the 2D grid.

Biologically, this aligns with cortical circuits, where modulatory neurons (e.g., interneurons, layer-specific cells) influence gain and oscillatory dynamics without directly relaying external stimuli (Watakabe et al., 2023). By enabling $o$ neurons to modulate local propagation kernels, BioOSS supports spatially varying dynamics—capabilities that single-field models like LinOSS lack.

### Distinctions from LinOSS and Neural Wave Machines (NWM)

**BioOSS** differs fundamentally from **LinOSS** and **NWM** in physical formulation, spatial structure, and frequency-selective modulation: LinOSS models second-order dynamics with global or optionally local coupling but lacks spatial structure, physical grounding, and a separation between signal and modulatory components. NWM introduces wave-like behavior via locally coupled oscillatory RNNs on structured grids, capturing cortical-like topography, but it is not based on PDEs and does not distinguish between signal and modulation. In contrast, **BioOSS** is derived from FDTD principles, using two interleaved fields to provide a physically and biologically grounded mechanism for localized propagation and modulation.

Moreover, $p-o$ coupling introduces learnable, frequency-selective resonance at each grid location, inspired by mixed selectivity in neural systems. This allows BioOSS to effectively model oscillatory and structured temporal patterns—an essential feature for rhythm-sensitive tasks.

### On the Inclusion of an Ablation Study

We agree that ablation studies and component-level justification are essential. Removing $o$ neurons disrupts the core design of BioOSS.

The two-field structure stems from the FDTD2D formulation, which inherently relies on interleaved fields to simulate wave behavior. $O$ neurons control key parameters such as propagation speed and damping. Removing them breaks the PDE structure and prevents simulation of wave propagation and modulation.

Additionally, BioOSS is discretized to remain compatible with the **scan** operator used in Structured SSMs. Removing $o$ neurons would necessitate a new recurrence rule incompatible with both FDTD and biological modularity.

To assess $o$ neurons’ contribution, we implement a simplified variant on shorter sequences and additional tasks:

- **Single Field**: Removes $o$ neurons, reducing the system to a diffusion-like update of the P-field. Input modulation and resonance are disabled.

#### Ablation Results

| Model         | sMNIST         | nsCIFAR-10      | ESC50-10ms      |
|---------------|----------------|------------------|------------------|
| Full BioOSS   | **98.1**       | **54.2**         | **35.0**         |
| Single Field  | 92.26 (-5.84)  | 37.91 (-16.29)   | 29.75 (-5.25)    |

The performance drop highlights the role of $o$ neurons in enabling spatially variant dynamics and frequency modulation, which single-field systems cannot capture. This supports both the modeling rationale and the empirical effectiveness of the architecture. 

## Major Concern 3: Unclear Derivation in Section 3

**Reviewer:** The derivation is difficult to follow.

**Response:** We acknowledge the confusion and will take the following actions:

- Clearly define the spatial domain of the neurons (2D grid) at the beginning of Section 3.
- Clarify when we move from continuous PDEs (Eq. 1–2) to the discretized system (Eq. 5–9), emphasizing that we work on a finite 2D lattice with fixed Δx.
- Improve Fig.1 by explicitly marking the grid resolution and denoting the discrete structure alongside the PDE formulation.

## Major Concern 4: No Demonstration of Traveling Waves

**Reviewer:** There is no evidence that BioOSS supports traveling waves; observed dynamics appear to be standing waves.

**Response:** While the visualizations in the current manuscript primarily show stationary patterns, BioOSS is formulated from a wave propagation PDE (via FDTD), which intrinsically supports traveling wave solutions. As such, the hidden layer dynamics inherently include both standing and traveling wave components.

In the current experiments, we focused on long-duration time-series tasks, where wavefront propagation is less visually salient than in spatially structured visual tasks. Long sequence lengths (several hundred time steps) make clear animations or frame-wise visualizations impractical. We will include a supplementary traveling wave visualization in a 2D setting.

## Major Concern 5: Justification of Not Including Transformer Baselines

**Reviewer:** The justification "Transformers are end-to-end" is incorrect. All models are end-to-end.

**Response:** We agree our phrasing was misleading. Our intent was to highlight fundamental architectural differences rather than training paradigms. BioOSS is designed to model local dynamical systems with explicit spatiotemporal continuity, grounded in oscillator-based dynamics. In contrast, standard Transformers rely on perceptron-based components and model global dependencies via attention mechanisms, without encoding spatiotemporal continuity or locality.

## Clarifications on Specific Reviewer Questions

### Q1: Connection to Watakabe et al. (2023) and Biological Motivation

**A1:** In *Watakabe et al.*, two key projection motifs in primate prefrontal cortex (PFC): (1) **patchy, columnar projections**, radially oriented and localized in submillimeter-scale patches, and (2) **diffuse projections**, which spread widely and contribute to gradient-based organization across the cortex. Both projection types are topographically structured, supporting spatially coherent cortical coordination.

Our BioOSS model was developed as a **computational abstraction** of these biological principles:

- **$p$ neurons** in BioOSS emulate the **columnar units** described in Watakabe et al., corresponding to localized clusters of pyramidal neurons, the main excitatory signal carriers. Arranged on a 2D grid, their local recurrence and frequency-specific oscillations capture the notion of **discrete processing modules** akin to patchy projections.

- **$o$ neurons** model the **lateral propagation dynamics**, inspired by **diffuse projections** that modulate activity across spatially distant areas. In our formulation, these $o$ neurons control wave propagation velocities, enabling low-amplitude, spatially distributed modulation that interacts with the localized oscillations of $p$ neurons. This provides a computational analogue to the diffuse projections described by Watakabe et al. (2023).

While we do not simulate anatomically resolved axonal arborizations, our model captures the functional consequences of both projection types: localized recurrent activity (patchy/columnar) and diffuse global modulations, jointly driving emergent dynamics. The "diffuse connectivity as modulation" interpretation suggested by the reviewer aligns well with our intent for the $o$ neuron population, and we appreciate the clarification opportunity.

### Q2: Justification of the Dynamical System and Role of $o$ Neurons

**A2:** This is addressed in Major Concern 2.

### Q3: Section 3.3 Too Detailed

**A3:** We agree. We will move much of Section 3.3 to the Appendix, retaining a high-level summary with the scan efficiency idea and eigen-decomposition rationale in the main text.

### Q4: Section 4.2 Lacks Relevance to Main Experiments

**A4:** Section 4.2 supports the theoretical foundation of BioOSS by validating its frequency-selective behavior and the eigenvalue frequency mapping in Section 3.5. By initializing spatial regions with distinct eigenmodes and applying identical white noise, we show that BioOSS generates region-specific oscillations consistent with their assigned bands. This confirms the theory and shows the model’s potential for EEG-like simulations, where each region can be selectively initialized. While spatial effects are harder to quantify, later experiments show hidden state frequencies align with or adapt to input signals. These findings demonstrate BioOSS’s capacity for rich oscillatory dynamics and mixed selectivity. We will move the full analysis to the Appendix and briefly explain its relevance in the main text.

### Q5: Clarify Train-Test Splits in UEA Tasks

**A5:** We followed Walker et al. [2024] and Rusch et al. [2024]'s 70:15:15 split. This is now clarified in Section 4.3.

### Q6: Section 4.3.2 Text Is Redundant with Tables

**A6:** Agreed. We will trim this section to avoid restating results and use the space for interpretation and ablation.

## 1. Related Work: Keller & Welling (Neural Wave Machines)

Due to space constraints, we focused the Related Work section on LinOSS and its foundational works. A similar concern was raised by another reviewer, and we plan to address this in the camera-ready version by expanding the discussion. The revised paragraphs below reflect our planned addition:

> Recent works have explored oscillatory and wave-like computation in neural systems, but differ significantly from BioOSS in their underlying mechanisms, biological grounding, and task domains.
> 
> Mechanistically, these models rely on matrix- or graph-based abstractions—such as masked recurrent matrices (e.g., Neural Wave Machines) or spectral graph filters (e.g., Balkenhol et al., 2024)—to simulate wave-like behavior. Physical implementations like Wave-RNNs (Hughes et al., 2019) and water-wave reservoirs (Maksymov, 2023) approximate wave propagation via analog substrates but lack a direct connection to physical wave equations.
> 
> In terms of biological grounding, many prior oscillatory models, such as coRNN (Rusch & Mishra, 2021), Neural Wave Machines (Keller & Welling, 2023), and Wave-RNNs, are built using generic RNN modules or abstracted couplings with no direct correspondence to cortical architecture. In contrast, BioOSS introduces signal-bearing $p$ and intermediate modulatory $o$ units, inspired by prefrontal microcircuits (Watakabe et al., 2023). Their interaction enables locally modulated wave propagation and a biologically plausible spatiotemporal abstraction.
> 
> Task-wise, most existing models are evaluated on static visual tasks, such as MNIST or image segmentation, which lack meaningful temporal dynamics (e.g., Liboni et al., 2023; Keller et al., 2024). BioOSS, in contrast, is explicitly designed for spatiotemporal sequence modeling and is evaluated on tasks that require long-range memory, frequency-based recognition, and dynamic signal tracking. Moreover, many oscillatory models, aside from LinOSS, do not provide a principled discretization scheme, making them difficult to integrate into structured state space modeling (SSM) frameworks. BioOSS is a discretized dynamical system with efficient Fourier-domain recurrence, compatible with modern SSMs.

NWM (Keller & Welling) targets visual tasks using recurrent spatially coupled architectures. While related, it is inspired by CoRNN and was not integrated into the common SSM architecture. However, we did experiment with NWM and Welling's subsequent models, applying them alongside BioOSS on visual and auditory datasets. Our FDTD2D structure, emulating wave propagation in brain-like media, yields richer oscillatory hidden states. **Table 1. Classification accuracy (%) on sMNIST, nsCIFAR-10, and ESC50-10 ms.** Comparison of **BioOSS** with other oscillatory models. |----------------|------------|----------------|----------------|
| NWM            | 98.6       | 56.2           | 6.8            |

| WaveRNN           | 97.6       | 55.0           | 18.8           |
| **BioOSS**     | 98.1       | 54.2           | 35.0           |

## 2. Section 3.2: Explicit Discretization Justification

In the final version, we will revise this section to better motivate why Section 3.2 includes a detailed derivation, rather than simply stating the use of a common Euler discretization. The key point is that standard formulations often use Euler updates implicitly, which prevents the construction of an explicit coupling matrix. This lack of explicit structure hinders the ability to apply backpropagation through the spatially coupled PDE system.

Our formulation makes the coupling matrix fully explicit and differentiable, which is crucial for enabling backpropagation in the PDE-based dynamics. We will move the derivation to the appendix and keep a concise version in the main text. We will also include a full algorithmic description of the update steps in the appendix to support reproducibility.

## 3. Architecture Clarification and Algorithm Update

We will revise Figure 1 to show the full model, including input/output layers, to better communicate how the PDE dynamics are embedded in the ML pipeline. **Algorithm 1: Training BioOSS with Spatio-Temporal Layer**

```
Input: Input sequence u  
Output: Output sequence s after L layers

for l = 1 to L do  
    // Step 1: Spatio-temporal PDE-based propagation  
    ∇p ← SpatialGradient(p)  
    ∇·o ← SpatialDivergence(o)  
    o* ← o - Δt·∇p  
    p* ← p - Δt·(c²⊙∇·o) + Δt·B·u
    o ← o* / (1+Δt·ko)  
    p ← p* / (1+Δt·kp)  
    x ← concat(p, o)  
    
    // Step 2: Linear projection and residual update  
    z ← Wz · x  
    gate ← σ(Wg · x)  
    x_out ← gate ⊙ tanh(z) + (1 - gate) ⊙ x_prev  
    
    // Step 3: Readout  
    y ← C · x_out + D · u  
    y ← GELU(y)  
    u ← GLU(y) + u_prev  
end for

Return final output s ← W_out · y + b_out
```

## 4. Clarification on Fourier Domain Use and Eigenstructure

The eigenstructure is used solely for theoretical analysis. Specifically, the matrix Λ contains the complex eigenvalues (mapped to frequency components), and P contains their associated eigenvectors. Though training is time-domain, we use $A = P \Lambda P^{-1}$ to:

- Analyze and visualize the frequency-selective behavior of each node.
- Justify the scan-efficient computation when approximated via block-wise diagonalization.

We will make this transformation and its purpose more explicit in Section 3.3.

## 5. Notation and Specific Line Fixes

- **Subscript/superscript consistency:** Inconsistencies (e.g., $k_p$, $k_o$) will be corrected throughout the manuscript.

- **Line 114–115:**  
The input’s time-dependency drives internal state changes in BioOSS via the term $M^{\text{Damp}^{-1}} F^{\text{Velocity}}$, which injects external stimuli at each step. While $M^{\text{Damp}^{-1}} M^{\text{Velocity}}$ governs spatial wave propagation—analogous to a reservoir—the input acts like a stone, triggering dynamic oscillations. The phrase “not effective” refers to **computational inefficiency**. To enable parallel scan operations, we extract local eigenvalues to construct a diagonalized transition matrix.  
**Revision:**  
We will revise the sentences as follows:  
> "Although $M^{\text{Damp}^{-1}} M^{\text{Velocity}}$ models internal propagation, it does not enable efficient temporal processing of input. Therefore, we extract local eigenvalues to construct a diagonal system matrix for parallel computation."

- **Line 118–121:**  
To clarify the inversion step in Line 118: since $M^{\text{Damp}}$ is diagonal by construction, its inverse can be directly computed by taking the reciprocal of the diagonal entries. The current explanation introduces unnecessary detail, assuming a more general block-diagonal case, which will be removed in future revisions.

- **Line 134:**  
The need for diagonalization via eigendecomposition $A = P \Lambda P^{-1}$ was not sufficiently motivated. The original transition matrix lacks associativity, limiting parallel computation. Inspired by Orvieto et al. (2023), we adopt eigendecomposition to obtain a diagonal matrix $\Lambda$, enabling scan operations for efficient recurrent updates and reducing the computational complexity from $\mathcal{O}(N)$ to $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$.  
**Revision:**  
We will add the following clarification:  
> "Following SSM literature (e.g., Orvieto et al., 2023, Rush et al., 2024), we apply eigendecomposition $A = P \Lambda P^{-1}$, where $\Lambda$ is a diagonal matrix. From Equation 16, eigenvalues λ₂,₃ form complex conjugate pairs. When mapped to the unit circle, they symmetrically align around the real axis. Therefore, the angular frequency associated with one eigenvalue corresponds to half a revolution over a sampling period, leading to the frequency estimate:

f = θ/(π Δt)

instead of θ/(2π Δt), as would be used in continuous-time systems. This formulation is consistent with our discrete-time eigenvalue interpretation.

## 7. Sensitivity of Hyperparameter

BioOSS is more sensitive to hyperparameters—particularly the learning rate—due to its complex internal structure. The model incorporates nonlinear, spatially localized connectivity through trainable damping and propagation dynamics, resulting in a highly non-smooth optimization landscape. As a result, suitable learning rates vary significantly across datasets and are typically much smaller than those used in other SSMs. This makes tuning more time-consuming and sensitive compared to standard models.

We will move the “Limitation” section to the appendix.

We would like to clarify that BioOSS does not aim to introduce a new oscillation-based state space model (SSM), nor is it framed as a contribution to the SSM family. Instead, we adopt SSM-compatible components as a practical means to explore how biologically grounded dynamics, particularly PDE-driven wave propagation, can be integrated into general-purpose modeling pipelines.

BioOSS is conceptually informed by prior work, especially LinOSS (Rusch and Rus, 2024), as reflected in the scan-based recurrence architecture. We have mentioned LinOSS over twenty times throughout the manuscript, including in the Introduction, Related Work, Methods, and Results. In the Related Work section, we only mentioned the closest model, LinOSS. Some reviewers have also recognized this connection. Although we did not apply hyperlink formatting to every mention, we are happy to provide clearer cross-referencing in relevant sections, such as the scan formulation and algorithm caption.

Our goal is not to reimplement or improve upon LinOSS, but to present a distinct approach grounded in a first-order PDE system that models wave dynamics over a 2D neural grid. This leads to a different form of spatio-temporal recurrence and biologically interpretable behavior, distinct from second-order ODE-based models.

Equations such as (17), (18), and the identity $\mathbf{P}\mathbf{P}^{-1} = \mathbf{I}$ are standard linear algebraic tools included for mathematical completeness and clarity, not specific borrowing. To prevent misunderstanding, we are open to clarifying the presentation or adding attribution notes.

In the final version, we will further emphasize how BioOSS diverges from LinOSS in its theoretical formulation, spatial structure, and modeling goals, while also improving clarity around citation and attribution.

## 1. Clarifying the Relationship to LinOSS

The apparent similarity arises from a scan-based recurrent architecture with gating mechanisms. However, we highlight several key distinctions:

- **Shared components are not unique to LinOSS:** Scan operations and gating are widely used in the state-space modeling literature (e.g., Mamba). These components are standard in the field and are adopted in BioOSS purely to ensure a fair and consistent comparison across models, particularly with LinOSS. We would like to emphasize that BioOSS does not claim to propose a novel oscillation-based SSM, nor is it positioned as a contribution to the SSM model family. Instead, our core innovation lies in formulating oscillatory dynamics from a biologically grounded partial differential equation (PDE) framework, which gives rise to distinct spatio-temporal behavior. To facilitate comparison with existing models, including those formulated in SSM form, we express parts of our architecture using SSM-compatible components. This design choice is practical and does not reflect the conceptual foundation of BioOSS, which remains independent of the standard SSM lineage.

- **Fundamental theoretical difference:** LinOSS is based on *forced linear second-order ODEs*, while BioOSS is derived from a *first-order PDE system* inspired by 2D wave propagation (FDTD2D). While LinOSS is a universal approximator of continuous causal operators, universality alone is not sufficient for modeling biologically realistic neural dynamics. BioOSS prioritizes spatially structured, frequency-selective, and interpretable dynamics grounded in cortical circuit motifs, such as lateral wave propagation and localized damping.

- **Spatio-temporal representation:** LinOSS uses 1D hidden vectors with no explicit spatial topology. BioOSS instead models a 2D grid of neurons with local interactions, enabling structured spatio-temporal processing aligned with biological cortical layers and spatial wavefront dynamics.

- **Discretization method differs:** BioOSS discretizes the first-order PDE using a hybrid Euler scheme, commonly used in wave propagation solvers such as FDTD. LinOSS derives its recurrence from implicit and IMEX solutions to a second-order ODE. This leads to distinct numerical properties, inductive biases, and biological interpretability.

- **Different scan application:** LinOSS uses scan along time with global hidden-to-hidden matrices. BioOSS applies the scan over a spatially-coupled operator derived from PDE eigenvalues, governing localized interactions across the grid.

- **Key distinctions in hidden-to-hidden coupling:** In **LinOSS**, the hidden-to-hidden matrix is a dense, learned matrix over feature dimensions, acting globally and uniformly across time. In **BioOSS**, the coupling matrix A governs local interactions across a 2D grid of neurons, derived from a physically grounded PDE and encoding wave propagation properties through meaningful parameters (c and k). BioOSS's recurrence is spatially structured and biologically interpretable, enabling localized oscillations and wavefronts.

## 2. Motivation and Formulation of the Coupling Mechanism

- **Biological inspiration:** Our model introduces distinct *primary neurons* and *intermediate neurons* inspired by cortical architectures. The coupling matrix is derived from FDTD-based wave propagation principles, using physically meaningful parameters: propagation speed (c) and damping (k).

- **Tunable local resonance:** The PDE-derived coupling allows BioOSS to adapt local oscillatory behavior via eigenvalues analytically determined by c and k, akin to tuning a frequency response.

- **Enhanced expressivity:** While LinOSS relies on temporal coupling alone, BioOSS offers spatio-temporal interactions essential for modeling wave-like behavior and frequency-specific propagation relevant in auditory and visual processing tasks.

## 3. Eigendecomposition, Diagonalization, and Scan Efficiency

- **Analytical diagonalization:** Our PDE formulation leads to a structured system matrix that is analytically diagonalizable. Closed-form eigenvalues are derived from c and k via spatial Fourier analysis, avoiding expensive numeric eigendecomposition.

- **Scan efficiency:** To efficiently implement parallel scan operations, we diagonalize the coupling matrix A via eigendecomposition: $ A^n = P \Lambda^n P^{-1} $. Here, $A$ denotes the trainable spatial coupling matrix governing recurrent dynamics across the 2D grid. The matrix $P$ transforms from the frequency domain to the physical (spectral) domain and is computed analytically, globally defined over the entire 2D hidden layer.

- **Approximation justified:** The eigendecomposition is based on a physically motivated linear approximation of the nonlinear PDE. While approximate, the parameters c and k are trainable, allowing backpropagation to correct for errors.

## 4. LinOSS Performance in Table 1

While we made every effort to reproduce LinOSS results using the official codebase and provided hyperparameters, we encountered challenges achieving the same performance. The repository lacks pre-trained checkpoints or explicit data splits, and available logs did not allow full reconstruction of the training pipeline. To ensure fair comparison, we re-evaluated all baselines under a unified pipeline and report the best reproducible results.

## 5. Theoretical Insights and Model Justification

BioOSS is grounded in a biologically interpretable PDE formulation, inspired by wave propagation in continuous media and the spatio-temporal dynamics of neuronal populations. Its trainable dynamics operate over a 2D grid, enabling localized oscillations and structured wavefronts.

Reviewer xBBL notes: "While biologically inspired, the model's structural complexity (2D grids, dynamic interactions) may pose challenges for scaling... The paper moves forward the field of oscillatory models." This highlights the conceptual novelty and depth of our work.

Our aim is not to outperform existing SOTA models but to assess whether biologically grounded dynamics, such as locally coupled wave propagation, can be integrated into general-purpose, scan-compatible architectures. These mechanisms, rooted in cortical computation, offer viable inductive biases for sequence modeling. While we incorporate SSM-compatible components for benchmarking and interoperability, these are implementation choices rather than conceptual foundations. The hidden state design, spatial organization, and theoretical derivation of BioOSS were independently developed and are fundamentally distinct from prior work, such as LinOSS.

rebuttal.value:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful feedback, which helped us clarify key aspects and identify promising future directions.

**Q1. Comparisons to state-of-the-art models (e.g., Transformers, Mamba) are needed to demonstrate practical utility and clarify when BioOSS effectively captures spatio-temporal correlations beyond benchmarks.**

**A1.**
We used the same setup as LinOSS for fair comparison among SSMs. In this configuration, Mamba underperformed S5 and LinOSS, so its results were omitted. On periodic time series datasets (Table 3), BioOSS does not outperform SOTA Transformers, though results remain acceptable. We thus focus comparisons within the SSM context. Moreover, MSE may not fully reflect model performance. For example, on regular rhythm datasets, BioOSS shows more biologically plausible dynamics (see analysis in A3).

Rather than chasing benchmarks, our goal is to propose a biologically grounded, interpretable framework based on 2D oscillatory wave propagation. Unlike Mamba and Transformer models, whose core building blocks are perceptron-style transformations with pointwise activations, BioOSS is governed by underdamped PDEs simulating traveling waves and resonant spatiotemporal behavior.

From a neuroscience perspective, mixed selectivity is a core principle of computation in cortical circuits [1], where diverse oscillatory responses arise from complex neural connectivity and are combined downstream for decision making and motor control. In this context, BioOSS’s oscillatory dynamics offer a biologically faithful substrate for learning. Resonant modes encode a distributed basis of temporal and spatial features, whose superposition enables flexible, compositional input representations.

This form of dynamic mixed selectivity is difficult to achieve with purely feedforward, perceptron-based models like Mamba or Transformers. Therefore, BioOSS offers a novel approach not just in terms of empirical benchmarks, but in its capacity to model the rich dynamical substrate of biological computation.

**Q2. How do structured local interactions among p and o neurons influence the emergence of wave-like propagation patterns, and how critical are these interactions for encoding temporal dependencies?**

**A2.** 
Specifically, the gradient of $p$ drives local changes in the velocity field $o$, while the divergence of $o$ determines how the pressure field $p$ evolves across the grid. These spatial operators are applied across a 2D lattice, allowing perturbations at a single point to propagate to neighboring nodes, thus forming traveling wavefronts.

The local interactions between $p$ and $o$ neurons are essential: the gradient of $p$ drives flow, and the divergence of $o$ redistributes activity across the grid. Together, these operators form a locally coupled system that supports oscillations, rather than pointwise recurrence.

Crucially, these oscillations persist in the system even after external input vanishes, due to the underdamped nature of the coupled PDE. This enables short-term memory to be maintained intrinsically by the system’s internal dynamics, without requiring explicit state storage or gating. Instead of vanishing instantly, the residual oscillations encode a compressed trace of past inputs, which can be retrieved and transformed by downstream layers.

In this way, the $p$–$o$ coupling is not only responsible for spatial signal propagation, but also acts as a mechanism for distributed temporal memory, where oscillations serve as transient carriers of recent history. To preserve the physical consistency of the FDTD formulation and maintain SCAN-compatible discretization, we did not ablate the $o$ field under the SSM framework. Instead, we introduced the hidden layer into an RNN setting and conducted a single-field ablation on visual and auditory tasks (see response to p2sQ for details).

**Q3. How robust is BioOSS to noisy, sparse, or irregularly sampled time-series data compared to other oscillatory or recurrent models?**

**A3.** 
BioOSS is expected to exhibit robustness to sparse or irregularly sampled inputs due to its oscillatory dynamics and spatially coupled structure. In particular, the damping term $k$ stabilizes the system, while the spatial gradient and divergence operators ensure distributed propagation of information across the grid.

Although this work does not explicitly evaluate irregular sampling, we previously applied a similar hidden layer to beat-based rhythm prediction tasks where the input time series was sparse, non-zero only at beat onsets, and zero elsewhere. Only our model retained beat memory after input ceased, producing an extra peak at the expected beat time. In contrast, baseline models such as LSTMs and Transformers failed to extrapolate beyond observed beats and did not show such predictive peaks.

These findings support the hypothesis that BioOSS’s oscillatory memory and spatial redundancy confer advantages in handling sparse temporal data. We see this as a promising direction for future work.

**Q4. Can you characterize mathematically the computation requirements?**

**A4.**
Yes. The computational cost of BioOSS primarily arises from its spatio-temporal update in the hidden layer, which is based on finite-difference approximations of a coupled PDE system. We characterize training and inference complexity as follows.

Let $p \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W}$ and $o = (o^x, o^y) \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times H \times W}$ denote the pressure- and velocity-like states defined on a 2D grid. At each time step, a BioOSS layer performs:

(a) Gradient update
$\nabla p_{i,j} = \left( \frac{p_{i,j} - p_{i,j-1}}{\Delta x},\ \frac{p_{i,j} - p_{i-1,j}}{\Delta x} \right)$

(b) Divergence update
$\nabla \cdot o_{i,j} = \frac{o^x_{i,j+1} - o^x_{i,j}}{\Delta x} + \frac{o^y_{i+1,j} - o^y_{i,j}}{\Delta x}$

(c) Damped update
$o^{(l)} = \frac{o^\ast}{1 + \Delta t \cdot k_o},\quad p^{(l)} = \frac{p^\ast}{1 + \Delta t \cdot k_p}$

These operations require $\mathcal{O}(HW)$ operations per layer per time step, where $H \times W$ is the spatial resolution of the 2D state.

Each layer also performs linear projections, gating, and readout on a hidden state of dimension $d=HW$ (number of $p$ neurons), yielding a cost of $\mathcal{O}(HW \cdot d)$.

Thus, the total inference cost per layer over $T$ time steps is:
$$
\mathcal{O}(L T H W d)
$$

During training, gradients must also be computed through the differentiable spatial operators and projection layers, with weight updates costing $\mathcal{O}(HW \cdot d^2)$ per layer. Therefore, the total training complexity is:
$$
\mathcal{O}(L T H W (d + d^2))
$$

In practice, the hidden layer dominates both inference and training cost, and the model’s complexity scales linearly with sequence length $T$, number of layers $L$, and spatial size $HW$.

**Q5. Can you state clearly where BioOSS clearly outperforms standard models—and why?**

**A5.**
Our primary objective is not to make incremental gains on benchmark performance, but to propose a biologically grounded, physically interpretable, and generalizable modeling framework based on oscillatory dynamics. BioOSS is designed to address three core challenges: interpretability, trainability of physically inspired systems, and architectural generalizability.

1. Interpretability via Biophysical Modeling

BioOSS simulates spatio-temporal neural activity on a 2D grid, analogous to the layout of cortical tissue. The dynamics are governed by finite-difference approximations of wave propagation (FDTD2D), reflecting how neural oscillations travel across brain tissue. This structure enables spatial frequency analysis and transparent interpretation, unlike abstract Transformer or RNN representations.

2. Trainability of Physically Realistic Oscillatory Systems

Unlike traditional models that are mostly based on perceptual or spike-based neuron abstractions, BioOSS employs a coupled PDE system with damped wave dynamics. While previous physically grounded models are difficult to train due to instability in backpropagation (especially through implicit solvers), our explicit Euler scheme ensures stability and differentiability for gradient-based training.

3. Generalizability beyond PDE Simulation

FDTD systems are typically used in constrained simulation settings and lack architectural flexibility. BioOSS overcomes this by embedding the wave dynamics as a differentiable hidden layer, enabling integration with SSM, RNN, or even attention-based architectures. Here, we focus on its SSM role for long-range modeling, where it matches SOTA models like S5 and LinOSS and outperforms them on harder datasets. However, the structure also supports variants with CNN or attention-based couplings, which we will test in separate experiments.

In sum, BioOSS does not aim to outperform every model on benchmark scores universally. Rather, it contributes a new modeling paradigm that is biophysically interpretable, mathematically grounded, and practically trainable, while maintaining competitive performance on general long-range sequence tasks.

**Q6. Is the interpretability gained from spatial frequency structure usable in downstream applications like clinical diagnostics or robotics?**

**A6.**
Yes, BioOSS’s frequency selectivity enables interpretability. We extract neuron-wise frequency responses from the eigenvalue spectra, revealing dominant low-frequency modes consistent with oscillatory behavior. These signatures could be used for downstream tasks such as identifying frequency-based biomarkers in neuroimaging or decoding sensory information in robotics.

Though our paper focuses on benchmarks, these dynamics have potential in broad downstream tasks. Future work will explore these directions.

[1] Rigotti, M., Barak, O., Warden, M. R., Wang, X. J., Daw, N. D., Miller, E. K., & Fusi, S. (2013). The importance of mixed selectivity in complex cognitive tasks. Nature, 497(7451), 585–590.

summary.value: The paper introduces BIoOSS, an extension of the recently proposed LinOSS model that incorporates locally coupled dynamics into the original framework.The paper provides an explanation how parallel scans can still be used for this framework and finally presents numerical results of BIoOSS mostly comparing it to the LinOSS model. However, the manuscript suffers from poor organization, lacks a clear motivation for introducing local coupling, and fails to demonstrate improved performance—especially when benchmarked against the originally published LinOSS results rather than the modified baselines reported in this paper (more in strengths and weaknesses).

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
* the paper extends a recently published model that has gained significant attention 
* the paper provides empirical results on various datasets

Weaknesses:
* The paper clearly extends and is fully based on the recently published LinOSS model of Rusch and Rus, 2024, e.g., the whole structure and representation follows the LinOSS paper almost verbatim. However, this is not explicitly stated and LinOSS is only cited twice before section 4 in the context of "other oscillatory models". I urge the authors to provide proper credit and clearly state that this works follows closely Rusch and Rus, 2024. 

* While BIoOSS does introduce coupling between nodes, the explicit formulation used in this manuscript lacks proper motivation. Why is this type of coupling used and not anything else? This is never explained nor motivated.

* It's not clear why coupling is needed for the LinOSS model. Rusch and Rus, 2024 have shown that LinOSS is universal. What functions/operators can BIoOSS express that LinOSS cannot? I presume there is none. Moreover, LinOSS does have coupling mechanism (otherwise it would not be universal). However, this is done in between layers, i.e., the dense input weight matrix modulates and couples the outputs from the layer before, which by definition is a coupling mechanism. Why is that not sufficient? There needs to be more explanations and analysis.

* The writing of the paper is poor, e.g., it's not clear how the underlying system is solved using parallel scans. In line 131-134: "This associativity is essential because it enables the use of parallel scan operations, reducing the computational complexity [...]. Therefore, we need to make the eigendecomposition [...]". How does the eigendecomposition help here? I presume the system is solved by diagonalizing it. However, this is never mentioned explicitly. 

* Line 155-156 says that P inverse only needs to be computed once. However, doesn't it need to be computed for every node i,j? How costly is that? Do you include it in the speed comparisons in the appendix?

* Table 1 provides weaker results for LinOSS than stated in the official LinOSS paper. This is very problematic. If one considers the originally published results of LInOSS, it performs much better (and not worse as stated in this manuscript) than BIoOSS (67.8\% for LinOSS vs 66.25\% for BIoOSS).

* The eigendecomposition provided is only an approximation. There is no further explanation or analysis provided how this affects the model behavior and performance.

* The paper does not provide any deeper or theoretical insights of this model nor lacks a clear motivation of why this particular model is chosen.

summary.value: This paper proposes a new model inspired by current oscillatory sequence models as well as neuroscience findings. It can be described using coupled PDEs, which can be solved efficiently in the Fourier domain, where the state evolution is linear and associative scans are applicable (which have $\log T$ time complexity). It reaches SOA performance on multiple tasks.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
**Results and Significance**


**Strenghts**: The results generally appear solid enough. On an appropriately chosen benchmark, the model outperforms existing architectures with comparable amounts of parameters and compute.

**Weaknesses**: The authors write that the model is very hyper parameter sensitive (line 421). It is unclear how much time was spent hyper-parameter tuning relative to the baseline models. In what fidelity was the learning rate (between 0.000001 and 0.005) explored?


**Clarity and originality**:


**Strengths**: The introduction is well written and nicely motivates the architecture 


**Weaknesses**: The writing can be improved in two points, namely:

*Comparison to previous work.* I think an important omission in the relation to previous work is from TA Keller & M Welling (on e.g., neural wave machines / traveling waves) which use a very similar setup of neuro-inspired oscillatory RNNs with spatial interactions (the latter being efficiently implemented with convolutions).

*Section 3.2 to 3.5 can be improved significantly in my opinion.* First of all it contains some elaborate details that can be moved to the appendix, for instance section 3.2 is an almost page long derivation, just to end up with a well known euler based integration scheme. On the other hand some essential details (even just a brief description), such as how the PDEs are used in an ML architecture (does the model contain multiple layers of these PDS with MLPs in between?) are omitted. Where/when do we transform back from Fourier domain to time domain?

**Minor**

- There are some inconsistencies in whether $o$ and $p$ are subscripts or superscripts of $k$ (and sometimes they are missing at all).
- I don´t understand line 114/115, how does the time-dependancy of the input play a role (or how is it addressed later?). 
- Line 118: isn’t this already diagonal by construction, why do we need to the intermediate block-diagonal step.
- Line 134, you have not explained why you want this diagonal matrix, maybe add something along the lines of “... so that we can perform the scan operation on the diagonalised transition matrix, similar to in Orvieto et al. 2023” 
- Line 178. I don’t understand why this is not $f =  \frac{\theta}{ 2 \pi dt}$.  A 2 dimensional linear system with c.c. eigenvalues with phase $\theta$ results in a sine and cosine trajectory with $f =  \frac{\theta}{ 2 \pi dt}$, no?

summary.value: The authors present a locally coupled oscillatory state space model with two populations of coupled neurons, governed by coupled PDEs. The authors evaluate the proposed model in Fourier space to allow for efficient recurrent computation through the well-known parallel associative scan operation. They evaluate the model's empirical performance on traditional sequence modeling tasks and demonstrate slightly improved performance over recent state of the art.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
**Strengths**
- The study of spatiotemporal computation in a computationally efficient manner is very welcomed and the proposed methodology appears sound. It is encouraging that the authors appear to have gotten this proposed model to work in the existing SSM context given that it is quite a complex model. 
- The inclusion of different types of neurons inspired by Watakabe et al. 2023 is an interesting novelty and improves the works originality and significance. 
- The stability analysis of Section 3.4 is a nice addition and appreciated. 
- The experimental results are promising although the benchmarks used are all small scale and known to be noisy.

**Weaknesses** 
- Related work section is extremely short and missing critical related work. Specifically the work of Keller & Welling (2023) (see citation below) explicitly builds a recurrent locally connected network of coupled oscillators for performing sequence modeling, also inspired by cortical spatiotemporal dynamics. Furthermore, this is far from the first work to build a computational model which leverages such dynamics, and the authors should acknowledge this in the paper and further describe how their current work differs. Without this comparison, the novelty and originality of their approach is very hard to discern. A non-exhaustive list of papers that the authors should both read and cite is listed below:
      - Hughes, T. W., Williamson, I. A., Minkov, M., & Fan, S. (2019). Wave physics as an analog recurrent neural network. Science advances, 5(12).
      - Rusch, T. K., & Mishra, S. (2021). Coupled oscillatory recurrent neural network (coRNN): An accurate and (gradient) stable architecture for learning long time dependencies. arXiv preprint arXiv:2010.00951. Retrieved from https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.00951.
	- Keller, T. A., & Welling, M. (2023). Neural wave machines: Learning spatiotemporally structured representations with locally coupled oscillatory recurrent neural networks. In Proceedings of the 40th international conference on machine learning. PMLR.
	-  Keller, T. A., Muller, L., Sejnowski, T., & Welling, M. (2024). Traveling waves encode the recent past and enhance sequence learning. In The twelfth international conference on learning representations. Retrieved from https:// openreview.net/forum?id=p4S5Z6Sah4
	- Balkenhol, J., Händel, B., Biswas, S., Grohmann, J., v. Kistowski, J., Prada, J., . . . Dandekar, T. (2024). Beyond- local neural information processing in neuronal networks. Computational and Structural Biotechnology Journal, 23, 4288-4305. Retrieved from https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S200103702400360X doi: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.csbj.2024.10.040
	- Jacobs, M., Budzinski, R. C., Muller, L., Ba, D., & Keller, T. A. (2025). Traveling waves integrate spatial information through time. arXiv preprint arXiv:2502.06034. Retrieved from [https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.06034](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.06034).
	- Maksymov, I. S. (2023). Analogue and physical reservoir computing using water waves. Retrieved from https:// arxiv.org/abs/2306.09095
	- Liboni, L. H. B., Budzinski, R. C., Busch, A. N., Löwe, S., Keller, T. A., Welling, M., & Muller, L. E. (2023, November). Image segmentation with traveling waves in an ex- actly solvable recurrent neural network. arXiv. Retrieved 2024-11-19, from http://arxiv.org/abs/2311.16943 (arXiv:2311.16943)
	- Effenberger, F., Carvalho, P., Dubinin, I., & Singer, W. (2025). The functional role of oscillatory dynamics in neocortical circuits: A computational perspective. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 122(4), e2412830122. Retrieved from https://www.pnas.org/ doi/abs/10.1073/pnas.2412830122 doi: 10.1073/pnas .2412830122
	- Even more work in the neural field theory literature... 
- Because of a lack of related work and ablations, it is not clear how different the proposed model is different from prior work. For example, it is not clear how the proposed model differs from an accelerated version (through parallel scan) of the Neural Wave Machine work. Similarly, it is not clear how the model differs from a locally-connected version of the LinOSS model. (Clearly the proposed model has an additional type of neuron with different dynamics, but the inclusion of this additional complexity is unjustified without results showing that it improves performance over the simpler alternative.)
- The definition and associated derivation of the model in section 3 is very hard to follow, despite the reviewer having experience with wave equations, and SSMs. Specifically, the space over which the neurons are defined should be stated before beginning with the derivation, and it should be made explicitly clear when switching from continuous to discrete spatial dimensions. 
    - Relatedly, equations 1 and 2 are a bit confusing because the image in figure 1 is defined over a discrete grid, while the equations appear to be implicitly defined over continuous space. These should be made explicit.
- There are no ablations for the proposed architectural components (such as the choice of two types of neurons), and the justification for the modeling choice is very limited (with really only a single reference to Watakabe 2023 for motivation). 
- Despite the authors claiming that their model supports traveling waves, there is no analysis or visualization which demonstrates this. The Figures in the main text and appendix depict what looks like standing waves in the corresponding frequency bands. 
- In the paper the authors write: "This paper primarily focuses on the exploration of oscillatory-based spatio-temporal model and sequential tasks. Therefore, we do not include Transformer models, as they are end-to-end frameworks". 
	- The use of the phrase 'end-to-end' here doesnt make sense. All of these models are end-to-end, and transformers are also used as sequence models, as the authors admit in the introduction, so the choice not to compare with Transformers appears more biased towards making their model look better rather than a true methodological difference.

questions.value:
- Can the authors expand on the connection of their model to the results of Watakabe et al 2023? From my reading of the paper, it is not precisely clear how their specific choice of P and O neurons has much relation to these results which instead describe diffuse/patchy connections based on their associated targets. The presented BioOSS model does not seem to recapitulate these two types of projections. Is the idea that the diffuse connectivity is the 'modulation'? And the columns are the P neurons? Where are the patchy connections in this model?

- Section 3.3 is too detailed for the main text and should largely be moved to the appendix in my opinion, with greater intuition for the proposed model and the resulting final equations in the main text. 

- Can the authors justify their choice of the particular dynamical system more explicitly? Either from the biological point of view, directly connecting it to natural observations (with explicit abstractions), or through ablation? For example, are the O neurons really necessary in this setup? What do they add that would be different from the Neural Wave Machine type of architecture, or LinOSS with local connectivity, for example? 

- Section 4.2 seems bizarrely out of place. What is the take-away from this analysis? It is clear that a dynamical system of oscillations will be dependant on the initalization, and a network of locally coupled oscillators will be dependant on connectivity eigenmode initalization. However this initalization does not appear relevant to any of the following experiments, and therefore seems to lack purpose in the text. I would suggest authors move this to the appendix in favor of including more related work, ablations, and justification for the model. 

- How were train-test splits for 4.3.1 chosen? This suite of tasks is known to be very specific to the choice of train-test split (from my own extensive experience with this data set).

- Section 4.3.2 text is largely repetitive of the tables in the section. There is no need to repeat the exact numbers from the table in the text. This can be removed to make more space for substantive material as discussed above.

final_justification.value: The paper presents an interesting method for spatiotemporal computing that fits within modern state space model frameworks for efficient training and inference. It has novelty in the use of two coupled populations of neurons, and the demonstrated results are promising. The related work is significantly lacking, but the authors have promised to fix this. They have explored additional ablations which improved the work.

title.value: BioOSS: A Bio-Inspired Oscillatory State System with Spatio-Temporal Dynamics

abstract.value: Today’s deep learning architectures are primarily based on perceptron models, which do not capture the oscillatory dynamics characteristic of biological neurons. Although oscillatory systems have recently gained attention for their closer resemblance to neural behavior, they still fall short of modeling the intricate spatio-temporal interactions observed in natural neural circuits. In this paper, we propose a bio-inspired oscillatory state system (BioOSS) designed to emulate the wave-like propagation dynamics critical to neural processing, particularly in the prefrontal cortex (PFC), where complex activity patterns emerge. BioOSS comprises two interacting populations of neurons: p neurons, which represent simplified membrane-potential-like units inspired by pyramidal cells in cortical columns, and o neurons, which govern propagation velocities and modulate the lateral spread of activity. Through local interactions, these neurons produce wave-like propagation patterns. The model incorporates trainable parameters for damping and propagation speed, enabling flexible adaptation to task-specific spatio-temporal structures. We evaluate BioOSS on both synthetic and real-world tasks, demonstrating superior performance and enhanced interpretability compared to alternative architectures.

Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).
